slides.title: Particulate Nature of Matter
slides.subtitle: You've gathered pebbles and sand on a riverbank. Where do they come from — and is a grain of sand the smallest a rock can get?
points: Why can you pile up sand or stones, but not a liquid like water?
We cannot see air, so how does it add weight to an inflated balloon?
Is the air we breathe today the same air that existed thousands of years ago?

slides.title: What is matter made of?
slides.intro: Where do pebbles and sand come from — and is a grain of sand the smallest a substance can get? Let's break things down to find out.

slides.title: From mountains to grains of sand
slides.body: High in the mountains, rocks slowly break down through **erosion**. Rivers carry the pieces along, grinding them into smaller pebbles, stones, sand, and clay. But is a single grain of sand the smallest piece of rock — or can it be broken further still?

slides.title: Keep breaking the chalk
slides.purpose: We want to find the **smallest piece** a substance can become. So we ask a simple question and test it: does chalk stay chalk, no matter how finely we grind it?
steps: Break — snap a stick of chalk, then break the pieces again
Grind — crush the bits to a fine powder with a mortar and pestle
Look — examine the powder through a magnifying glass
slides.observe: Every speck is **still chalk** — grinding changes only the **size**, never the substance. That hints matter is built from **tiny basic units** we simply haven't reached yet.

slides.title: What if you never stopped grinding?
slides.body: Grinding chalk is only a **physical change** — the size shrinks, but it stays chalk. Now imagine you keep going and never stop. Eventually you'd reach tiny units that **cannot be broken any further** — the basic building blocks the chalk is made of.

slides.title: These are constituent particles
slides.body: A **constituent particle** is the basic unit that makes up a larger piece of any substance — and one stick of chalk holds a huge number of them. It isn't only chalk: the grains of sand and clay are themselves built from countless constituent particles too.

slides.title: Where does the sugar go?
slides.purpose: Sugar seems to 'disappear' into water — but does it really vanish? We test whether something can still be **present even when we can't see it**.
steps: Add — stir two spoons of sugar into a glass of water until it vanishes
Taste — try a spoonful from the top layer
Repeat — try the same with sand instead of sugar
slides.observe: The water tastes **sweet**, so the sugar is still there — each grain broke into **millions of particles** too small to see, which slipped into the **gaps between the water particles**. Sand, held together more strongly, stays whole and settles.

slides.title: Into the spaces between particles
slides.body: The sugar didn't disappear. Its tiny particles **separated and slipped into the gaps** between the water particles. These gaps between constituent particles are called **interparticle spaces** — and they hold the key to how matter behaves.

slides.title: What decides the state of matter?
slides.intro: Solid, liquid, or gas — what sets them apart? The answer is the pull between particles and the space between them.

slides.title: Particles pull on one another
slides.body: Constituent particles are held together by **interparticle attractions**. Their strength depends on the substance and on the **distance** between particles — even a slight increase in distance weakens them sharply. This strength is what decides whether matter is a solid, a liquid, or a gas.

slides.translation: Thousands of years ago, the Indian philosopher Acharya Kanad reasoned that all matter is built from tiny, indivisible, eternal particles — long before microscopes could show us anything so small.

slides.title: Solid state
slides.intro: Why does a solid keep its shape no matter how you turn it?

slides.title: Hammer a nail, a stone, a key
slides.purpose: Why does a solid keep its shape? We handle and strike everyday solids to feel **how strongly their particles are held together**.
steps: Collect — an iron nail, rock salt, a stone, wood, a key, aluminium
Observe — the shape and size of each
Hammer — try to change their shape
slides.observe: Each object keeps its **own shape and size** and resists the hammer. In a solid, particles are **packed tight and held strongly** in fixed places — they can only vibrate, not move past each other — so shape and volume stay definite.

slides.title: Tightly packed, locked in place
slides.body: In a solid the particles are **tightly packed** with **strong** attractions, so they sit in fixed positions. They can only **vibrate** to and fro — they cannot slip past one another. That is why a key or a stone holds its shape no matter how you turn it.

slides.title: Vibrate, weaken, melt
slides.body: Heat a solid and its particles **vibrate more and more vigorously**. At a certain point the vibrations grow so strong that particles break free of their fixed places, the attractions weaken, and the solid turns to liquid. That temperature is the **melting point**.

slides.title: Weak forces melt easily; strong forces resist
Heat it up and watch
slides.caption: Drag the temperature: particles gain energy, break free of their fixed places, and spread out — solid to liquid to gas.

slides.title: Liquid state
slides.intro: A liquid flows and takes any shape — but does it keep a fixed amount?

slides.title: Pour the same water, A to B to C
slides.purpose: Does a liquid have a fixed shape? A fixed amount? We move the **same water** through differently shaped containers to find out.
steps: Mark — the 200 mL level in three differently shaped containers
Pour — move the water from A to B to C
Watch — its shape and its level each time
slides.observe: The water **takes on each container's shape**, yet the level reads **200 mL** every time. So liquids have **no fixed shape but a definite volume** — their particles move freely, but stay close together.

slides.title: No fixed shape, but a fixed volume
slides.body: Liquids **take the shape** of their container because their particles are free to move — yet the volume never changes. Their attractions are a little **weaker than in solids**, but still strong enough to keep particles close. Move a finger through water and it just closes back up.

slides.title: From liquid to vapour
slides.body: Heat a liquid and its particles move so vigorously that they **escape** into the air as vapour. The temperature where this happens fast, with bubbles forming throughout, is the **boiling point**. Below it, particles still slip off the surface slowly — that slower process is **evaporation**.

slides.title: Gaseous state
slides.intro: Give a gas more room and it just keeps spreading. Why?

slides.title: Trap smoke in a jar
slides.purpose: Does a gas hold a shape or a volume of its own? We trap smoke and then give it **more space** to see where it goes.
steps: Collect — catch incense smoke inside one gas jar
Stack — invert a second, empty jar on top of it
Watch — where the smoke travels
slides.observe: The smoke **spreads to fill both jars** completely. Gas particles feel **almost no attraction**, so they move freely and spread to fill **all the space** available — gases have no fixed shape or volume.

slides.title: Free to roam, filling all space
slides.body: In a gas the attractions are **negligible**, so particles move freely in every direction and spread to fill whatever space they are in. Because both liquids and gases **flow** and hold no fixed shape, we group them together and call them **fluids**.

slides.title: How interparticle spacing differs
slides.intro: Why can you squeeze air but not water? It comes down to the gaps between particles.

slides.title: Squeeze a sealed syringe
slides.purpose: Why can you squeeze air but not water? We compress each one to compare **how much empty space** sits between their particles.
steps: Seal — pull the plunger out, block the tip with your thumb
Push — press the plunger in, first with air inside
Repeat — now fill it with water and push again
slides.observe: Air **compresses** and the plunger slides in; water **barely moves**. Gas particles sit **far apart** with room to close up, while liquid particles are already **packed close** — so liquids are almost incompressible.

slides.title: Gas particles have room to spare
slides.body: Air squeezes because gas particles sit **far apart**, with plenty of space to close up. Water resists because its particles are already **packed close**. Even in solids a little space remains between particles — and, surprisingly, it holds **nothing at all**, not even air.

slides.title: How particles move
slides.intro: Are particles sitting still, or always on the move? A drop of colour will tell us.

slides.title: A grain of colour spreads on its own
slides.purpose: Are particles sitting still, or always moving? We drop a colour into **perfectly still** water — no stirring at all — and simply watch.
steps: Drop — a grain of potassium permanganate into still water
Watch — the pink streaks creep out from the grain
Wait — without stirring, and keep watching
slides.observe: With no stirring, the colour spreads until the **whole glass is evenly pink**. The water particles are in **constant motion** — they pull the colour off the grain and keep hitting it, scattering it everywhere.

slides.title: Particles never sit still
slides.body: The water particles **pull the colour off** the grain and keep **hitting** it, scattering it everywhere. Add heat and they move even faster — the colour spreads **fastest in hot water**, slowest in ice-cold. Light an incense stick and moving **air particles** carry its scent across the whole room the same way.

slides.title: How soap lifts away oil
slides.body: The particulate nature of matter even washes your clothes. A **soap particle** has two ends: one **grips the oil** stuck to the fabric, while the other **mixes with water** — so the oil is pulled off the cloth and rinsed away.

slides.title: Heat decides the state of matter
slides.body: It all comes down to **thermal (heat) energy**. Low energy keeps particles close, with strong attractions and only tiny vibrations — a **solid**. Add energy and they loosen into a **liquid**, then break free into a freely moving **gas**.

slides.title: The particles have names
slides.body: These tiny particles are **atoms** and **molecules**. Iron is made of iron atoms, gold of gold atoms. Some atoms — like hydrogen and oxygen — don't live alone but join into **molecules**: two hydrogen atoms make a hydrogen molecule, and water is two hydrogen atoms bound to one oxygen.

slides.title: Words from this chapter
slides.body: The vocabulary of the particle world:

slides.title: Everything is particles in motion
slides.subtitle: From a riverbank pebble to a fragrance crossing the room — the unseen dance of tiny particles, and the heat that drives it, explains all the matter around you.
